activities.anchor: the rational maximiser is a model, not a person
activities.caption: which bias drives each behaviour?
activities.name: beBiasSort

items.label: a judge's sentence is harsher after rolling a high number
'was £60, now £39' makes the deal feel like a win
a shopper won't sell a mug for £5 but won't buy one for £5
the same person buys insurance and a lottery ticket
a saver takes £100 today over £110 tomorrow
a student vows to save, then spends the money on a night out

config.why: All three are directional and predictable: first numbers drag estimates, losses loom larger than gains, and the present is discounted steeply.

config.prompt: In Prelec and Simester's MIT auction, credit-card users bid up to roughly twice as much as cash payers for the same basketball tickets. By what percentage did their bids run higher?
config.why: Twice as much is 100% higher. Plastic decouples purchase from payment, dulling the pain of paying.
config.context: the tickets were identical; only the payment method changed

activities.anchor: loss aversion just means people are risk-averse
activities.caption: one curve, two signs — trace the fourfold pattern
activities.name: beFourfoldBranch

config.root: A certain loss of £800, or an 85% chance of losing £1,000. Then the same choice in gains. Trace what prospect theory predicts.

start.text: Which do most people choose for the loss?

choices.label: Gamble on the 85% chance of losing £1,000
choices.feedback: Yes — over likely losses, people become risk-seeking.

choices.label: Take the certain £800 loss
choices.feedback: That is what a risk-averse expected-utility maximiser would do; most people gamble here.

loss.text: Now flip the sign: a sure £800 gain, or an 85% chance of £1,000?

choices.label: Take the sure £800
choices.feedback: Yes — over likely gains, the same person turns cautious.

choices.label: Gamble for £1,000
choices.feedback: Most take the sure gain; the risk-seeking is reserved for losses.

gain.text: One curve predicts both: risk-averse over likely gains, risk-seeking over likely losses. That fourfold pattern is why the same person buys insurance and lottery tickets.

sure.text: Standard risk aversion would take the certain loss, but the evidence says most people gamble to avoid it.

gamble.text: Most people take the sure gain in the gain frame; the pattern flips with the sign.

config.why: Loss aversion is defined relative to a reference point; the fourfold pattern flips risk attitude with the sign and likelihood, which plain risk aversion cannot predict.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the planner and the doer
activities.name: bePresentCloze

config.text: People take £100 today over £110 tomorrow, yet happily wait a year for the extra £10 — a pattern called %%0%% discounting. It makes preferences time-%%1%%, so the morning's planner and tonight's %%2%% disagree. Commitment devices and defaults bind the doer to the planner's intention.
config.hint: Patience depends on distance from the present; the planner makes the plan, the doer spends the money.

activities.anchor: is the cleanest evidence: one player proposes
activities.caption: find the ultimatum-game slip
activities.name: beUltimatumSpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the ultimatum-game reasoning goes wrong:
lines: A proposer splits £10 and offers the responder £2.
The responder rejects the offer, so both players get nothing.
Because rejection destroys value, it proves the responder is simply irrational.
Across experiments, offers below about 30% are routinely rejected.
That costly punishment is a stable social preference, predictable enough to model.
config.correction: Rejection is costly but predictable: responders punish unfair splits, and that preference is stable enough to model.
config.why: Behavioural economics widened what maximisation is over; it did not abolish rationality.

config.prompt: Flyvbjerg's sample found rail projects overran budgets by around what percentage on average? Place it.
config.why: Rail averaged about 45% over budget and roads about 20%. Reference-class forecasting uses that outside record instead of the project's special story.

activities.anchor: the classic teaching example is the airline's
activities.caption: sell the standby seat — marginal logic in order
activities.name: beSunkOrder

config.prompt: A near-empty flight is about to leave. Put the marginal argument for selling a standby seat in order:
items: The flight is already going, so its fixed costs are sunk
The marginal cost of one more passenger is about £20 in fuel, catering and fees
A standby fare of £40 adds £20 of contribution
Average cost per seat (£400) is irrelevant to this decision
Automating the sale down to the marginal margin captures the gain
config.why: Only forward-looking costs and benefits matter; anchoring on average cost refuses a sale that adds £20.

activities.anchor: price itself is a psychological object
activities.caption: pair each pricing tactic with its mechanism
activities.name: bePriceMatch

config.prompt: Pair each pricing tactic with its mechanism:

pairs.right: £39 outsells £34 because the left digit dominates
'was £60, now £39' makes the deal feel like a gain
a dominated print-only option pushes buyers to print-plus-web
snowstorm shovel price rises are judged unfair, and customers retaliate

config.why: Each works on the reference point, the comparison set or the norm — which is why regulators police fake 'was' prices.

activities.caption: where competition cures bias, and where it amplifies it
activities.name: beMarketsCompare

config.prompt: Where competition cures bias, and where it amplifies it — drag the divider:

before.label: product markets
before.text: fast feedback and personal consequences: a supermarket that systematically misprices bread loses customers, so biases are disciplined

after.label: asset markets
after.text: delayed, social feedback: traders told the fundamental value still bubble and crash, so biases are amplified

config.why: The same brains behave differently by environment; that asymmetry is why policy attention has shifted toward financial stability.

activities.caption: true or false — the replication reckoning
activities.name: beReplicationJudge

statements.s: Many early social-priming findings failed to replicate, and the field responded with pre-registration and larger samples.
statements.why: The Open Science Collaboration reproduced under half of 100 psychology studies, forcing a methodological reset.

statements.s: The sturdiest behavioural results — loss aversion, present bias, default effects — did not survive replication scrutiny.
statements.why: They did survive, which is precisely why they anchor this lesson.

statements.s: Expertise debiases specific, practised decisions rather than the decision-maker in general.
statements.why: List's card traders learned their market; the same people still show biases on unfamiliar choices.

statements.s: A striking single experiment should be trusted until someone bothers to replicate it.
statements.why: The replication reckoning says the opposite: ask whether it has replicated, at scale, out of the lab.
